newsitem.title: FRANCE: Farmers face curbs, want cash to tackle drought.
newsitem.headline: Farmers face curbs, want cash to tackle drought.

text.p: French authorities told grain growers on Tuesday to turn down the taps for two days a week as farmers in Britain faced a clampdown on irrigation due to fears of a drought in western Europe.
In Portugal, farmers warned they might appeal to the government for cash to aid producers in the southeast who are already battling drought.
A spell of several weeks without rain has encouraged farmers to tap directly into underground reservoirs to sprinkle parched crops, raising fears of water shortages.
Authorities in provinces around Paris have ordered farmers to suspend irrigation for 48 hours each weekend, probably starting from this Saturday, a local government official said.
The bread-basket region provides a sixth of France's wheat crop, the largest in Europe and a major French export earner.
In Britain farmers in East Anglia also faced the possibility of restrictions on water usage.
"It's probable, rather than possible, that restrictions will be widespread," a spokesman for the Environment Agency said.
Rainfall in the major grain-producing region over the last two years has been the lowest on record, leaving groundwater levels precariously low.
Portugal's main farmers' group said rainfall levels had been very low over the past three months, and it had not rained at all in March for the first time in more than a century.
"We are studying the matter closely and may decide to ask the government to activate the 'calamities fund'," a senior official with the Confederation of Portuguese Farmers said.
Local reports said farmers in the Alentejo, who produce most of Portugal's wheat and barley, had already lost much of their crops.

Despite the discomfort, experts said they were wary of predicting serious damage to Europe's harvest or a return to high prices this year. There was still plenty of time for crops to recover before the summer harvest, French analysts said.
This time last year farmers faced a similar threat but still managed to produce a record European Union wheat crop of 91 million tonnes.
Farmers have boosted sowings this year to take advantage of looser EU planting rules, helping prices to stabilise at around half the record levels seen a year ago when stocks were extremely low.
But even without irrigation restrictions, some farmers will struggle to make up for the stress already placed on their autumn-sown crops, a French farm ministry source said.
"It is extremely dry. There are problems. The crops are suffering from lack of water," the source said.
The problem spread to grain importing areas this week as Algeria installed a task force to draw up a programme of water rationing and cut down waste to save water for agriculture.
Government newspaper El Moudjahid on Monday, quoting a ministerial report, said rainfall coinciding with the most sensitive period for cereals was 70 percent below average.
Despite having a large grain crop, Algeria is one of the main importers of European wheat to feed its 29 million people.
